answers.answer: Shuffle the nine region cards; reveal the top card and place the King there. Each player takes another card for their home region and places their Grande there. Each starts with ten Caballeros: two beside the Grande in the home region, one on the first success-track space, and seven in their court.
answers.evidence: Setup: “two in their home region beside the Grande, one on the first space ... and seven in their court.”

answers.answer: In round 1, the players choose who starts. In later rounds, the player who took the last turn in the preceding round starts. Others play clockwise, and no power-card value already played that round may be matched.
answers.evidence: Turn Structure: “later, the player who took the last turn in the preceding round begins”; “Others play clockwise”; “No value already played this round may be matched.”

answers.answer: Players take turns in descending power-card value. At the start of a turn, recruit up to the number shown on that power card from the provinces into court; recruiting fewer is allowed. Recruitment happens before choosing an action card.
answers.evidence: Turn Structure: “At the start of your turn recruit up to the number ... from the provinces into your court”; then “After recruitment, choose an available face-up action card.”

answers.answer: If your provinces lack enough of your color, you may take your own Caballeros from the board to make up the difference. The King’s region is taboo, and the Castillo cannot supply pieces outside general scoring.
answers.evidence: Turn Structure: “you may take your own from the board to make up the difference”; “The King’s region remains taboo and the Castillo cannot supply pieces outside general scoring.”

answers.answer: Ordinary deployment moves up to the action card’s number from your court to regions adjacent to the King’s current region and/or the Castillo, with the allowance dividable freely. It cannot be split into separate parts around another activity (see Q06), but can be divided among destinations. The printed allowance is a maximum; you may deploy fewer or none.
answers.evidence: Actions: “number is a maximum”; “may deploy fewer, including none”; “dividing the allowance freely.”

answers.answer: Yes. Ordinary deployment and the special action may be done in either order, but each must be completed as a whole before starting the other; neither may be split or interleaved. You may decline the special action.
answers.evidence: Turn Structure: “Do them in either order ... neither may be split or interleaved”; “You may decline the special action.”

answers.answer: After a turn, lay the selected action card aside so later players cannot choose it. After everyone has taken a turn, discard remaining face-up action cards. The King card is revealed again every round and is never permanently discarded.
answers.evidence: Turn Structure: “Lay aside the selected action card”; “discard any remaining face-up action cards”; “King card ... never permanently discarded.”

answers.answer: No Caballero, Grande, or mobile scoreboard may move into or out of the King’s region; it may still be scored. Moving the King changes which region is protected.
answers.evidence: Protected locations: “no Caballero, Grande or mobile scoreboard may move into or out of it. ... It may still be scored. Actions that move the King are the exception.”

answers.answer: Clearly announce how many Caballeros you put in the Castillo. They may enter regardless of the King’s location. They may leave only during general scoring; no action removes them.
answers.evidence: Actions: “Announce clearly how many you put inside”; “regardless of the King’s location”; “leave only during general scoring.”

answers.answer: General scoring occurs after rounds 3, 6, and 9. In order: (1) each player secretly chooses one destination region for all their Castillo Caballeros, setting a face-down disk before the Castillo is uncovered; (2) uncover and score the Castillo; (3) reveal disks and move all Castillo Caballeros to the chosen regions, then replace the empty Castillo; (4) score the nine regions in scoring-track order and record points.
answers.evidence: General scoring: “Secretly select destinations before uncovering the Castillo”; then score Castillo, reveal disks/empty Castillo, and score nine regions. Overview gives rounds 3, 6 and 9.

answers.answer: A player must send all their Castillo Caballeros to one region, not split them. The King’s region is prohibited as a destination, and no pieces may be kept in the Castillo after its general scoring. If a player illegally chose the King’s region, their pieces go to their court; that consequence does not make the choice permitted.
answers.evidence: General scoring: “All that player’s Castillo Caballeros must go to one region”; “Choosing the King’s region is prohibited”; illegal choice sends pieces to court; Castillo is replaced empty.

answers.answer: The three players tied at four each receive second-place value, 3 points each; the player with three receives third-place value, 1 point. Grandes do not count toward majority; only Caballeros count.
answers.evidence: Example: “4,4,4,3 score 3,3,3,1”; “Only Caballeros count toward majority. A Grande ... contributes zero Caballeros.”

answers.answer: The player with four receives 6 points; the player with three receives 4; each player with two receives 0.
answers.evidence: Publisher scoring example: “On 6/4/2, counts 4,3,2,2 score 6,4,0,0.”

answers.answer: In a two-player game only first place can pay; in a three-player game first and second can pay. A tie for first shifts to second-place value, but the two-player cutoff then means neither player scores.
answers.evidence: Region ranks: “Two players: only first place can pay. Three players: only first and second can pay”; “a two-player tie for first pays neither player.”

answers.answer: Whenever the relevant region is scored, including special scoring, the sole majority holder in the King’s region gets +2, and the sole majority holder with their own Grande in a region gets +2. Neither bonus is awarded on a tie for first.
answers.evidence: Bonuses: apply “whenever the relevant region is scored, including special scorings”; each is +2; “Neither bonus is awarded on a tie for first.”

answers.answer: Specially scoring the Castillo reveals and scores its pieces, then covers those same pieces again. It does not empty or redistribute them; they leave only at general scoring.
answers.evidence: Actions: “Special scoring of the Castillo reveals and scores its contents, then covers them again without redistribution.”

answers.answer: A mobile scoreboard may be placed at the Castillo. It may not move into or out of the King’s region, the two scoreboards may not be stacked, and they may not be reversed or rotated to change their values.
answers.evidence: Stack 4: Castillo allowed; “No movement into or out of the King’s region”; “cannot be stacked”; place right side up, never reversed or rotated.

answers.answer: You may move your Grande to another region except the King’s region or Castillo; a Grande in the King’s region cannot leave. The destination may already contain several Grandes. The destination becomes your new home region.
answers.evidence: Stack 4—Grande: “another region except the King’s region or Castillo”; destination may already contain several Grandes; “destination becomes your new home region.”

answers.answer: Return any one of your played power cards to your hand, including the one played this turn. You need not reveal which card you choose, although taking the visible top card is apparent.
answers.evidence: Stack 4—Power Cards: “any one ... including the one played this turn”; “You need not reveal which.”

answers.answer: The game ends after all stages of the third general scoring, after round 9. The player furthest along the success track wins.
answers.evidence: End: “Finish all stages of the third general scoring, after round 9”; furthest along the success track wins.

answers.answer: Separate the action cards into stacks by the 1–5 Caballeros printed on their backs, shuffle each stack separately, and place them face down beside the board. At the start of each round, reveal the top card of each of the five stacks (five choices). The standard round marker starts at 1.
answers.evidence: Setup: stack by 1–5, shuffle separately; round marker at 1. Turn Structure: reveal top card of each of five action stacks.

answers.answer: A played power card is not returned to hand; it remains in that player’s face-up used stack, with only the top card visible. A special action can recover a played card.
answers.evidence: Turn Structure: “Played cards remain in each player’s face-up used stack with only the top card visible”; special action can recover one.

answers.answer: If the King card’s special action is done before ordinary deployment, the King’s new position determines the adjacent destinations. The King may be placed in any region except the Castillo.
answers.evidence: King card: put King in “any region except Castillo”; use current location at time of deployment. Protected locations: moving King first means use new position.

answers.answer: Keep the Veto card before you to retain it. It can stop one special action during this round or the next, but cannot stop the ordinary deployment portion of an action card.
answers.evidence: Stack 2—Veto: “Put the card before you and retain it”; stops one special action; “It cannot stop the ordinary deployment portion.”

answers.answer: While you hold Veto, other players must announce special actions before executing them. Object as soon as the player starts: you can stop an announced action before execution or prevent the remaining part of an incomplete special action. A completed action cannot be vetoed, and already executed parts are not undone; you may stop just part.
answers.evidence: Veto: players “must announce special actions before executing them”; object “as soon as the player starts”; completed actions cannot be vetoed and executed parts are not undone.

answers.answer: Discard Veto after using it once. If unused, discard it at the end of the next round.
answers.evidence: Veto: “Discard after using the veto once; if unused, discard at the end of the next round.”

answers.answer: Every fellow player sends all Caballeros in their court to the provinces; the selecting player is unaffected. A fellow player with an empty court sends none.
answers.evidence: Decay of Authority—all court: “Every fellow player sends all Caballeros in their court to the provinces”; “an empty court sends none”; selecting player unaffected.

answers.answer: The fellow player with two sends both, since they send all they have if fewer than three. You are unaffected and keep your five.
answers.evidence: Decay of Authority—three from court: “three ... or all they have if fewer than three”; selecting player unaffected.

answers.answer: The detailed execution paragraph and matching card face require each player, including the selecting player, to send three of their own Caballeros to the provinces. Start with the player to the selecting player’s left, proceed clockwise, and have the selecting player go last. Each chooses their pieces from any regions and/or their court, but not the King’s region or Castillo. The summary says the source gives no explicit shortfall rule if a player has fewer than three eligible pieces. The bold heading instead says “fellow players.”
answers.evidence: Stack 2—The King returns: detailed paragraph/card says each player including selecting player sends three; stated order and source exclusions; heading says “fellow players.”

answers.answer: The selecting player chooses one Caballero from a region for each player, including themselves, and returns each to its owner’s provinces. Pieces cannot be taken from courts, the King’s region, or Castillo.
answers.evidence: Send one from each player: selecting player chooses one “for each player, including themselves”; no taking from courts, King’s region, or Castillo.

answers.answer: Each affected fellow player secretly selects a region on their disk, with choices simultaneous and revealed together. A player who has at least one legal region containing two or more of their own Caballeros must choose a region containing at least two of their Caballeros. The King’s region and Castillo are excluded.
answers.evidence: Secretly remove two: simultaneous secret disk selection, reveal together; choose a region with at least two of that player’s Caballeros; never take from King’s region or Castillo.

answers.answer: If they have at most one in every region, the stated singleton fallback is to choose a region with one and return that one to the provinces.
answers.evidence: Secretly remove two: “The stated singleton fallback applies if the player has at most one in every region: choose a region with one and return that one.”

answers.answer: Each affected fellow player secretly chooses a region containing at least one of their Caballeros on a disk; choices are simultaneous and revealed together. They return all their own Caballeros there to the provinces. A player with none in any region is unaffected.
answers.evidence: Secretly remove all from one region: simultaneous secret disk selection; choose a region with at least one; return all their own there; player with none is unaffected.

answers.answer: Yes, choose any region, including the King’s region, or the Castillo. Use normal region-scoring rules, applicable rank limits and bonuses. If Castillo is chosen, score and cover the same pieces again; they are not redistributed.
answers.evidence: Pick one region: any region including King’s region or Castillo; normal rules and bonuses; Castillo pieces covered again without redistribution.

answers.answer: The printed 4-value group is Galicia (4/2/0), Catalonia (4/2/1), and Seville (4/3/1). Eligibility is determined by a region’s current first value, so Galicia with 8/4/0 does not qualify and Granada with 4/0/0 does. Applicable bonuses apply to special scorings.
answers.evidence: Stack 3—all 4-value regions: current first value determines group; mobile example says 8/4/0 in Galicia removes it and 4/0/0 in Granada adds Granada. Bonuses apply to special scorings.

answers.answer: The printed 5-value group is Basque Country (5/3/1), Aragon (5/4/1), and Valencia (5/3/2). The printed 6-and-7 group is Old Castile (6/4/2), New Castile (7/4/2), and Granada (6/3/1). For both cards, current first value determines eligibility, so mobile scoreboards can remove a printed member or add another region. Castillo is explicitly not scored by the all-5 card.
answers.evidence: Stack 3 lists the printed groups and says current first value determines 5 or 6/7 eligibility; “Castillo is not scored” for all-5.

answers.answer: Only sole first places score; all lower ranks score nothing. A tie for first scores nothing because it would normally pay second place. Castillo is excluded.
answers.evidence: First position only: “only sole first places score”; tie for first scores nothing; “Excludes Castillo.”

answers.answer: Score all board regions tied for the most total Caballeros. Do not consider or score the Castillo, even if it contains more than either tied region.
answers.evidence: Most-Caballeros card: “Score all regions tied for the most”; “Castillo is neither considered nor scored.”

answers.answer: Compare nonempty board regions and score all regions tied for the least. Empty regions are excluded, and the Castillo is neither considered nor scored.
answers.evidence: Least-Caballeros card: “Compare nonempty board regions; score all tied for the least. Empty regions and Castillo are neither considered nor scored.”

answers.answer: All fellow players move all their own Caballeros out of the chosen region. Each affected player secretly chooses another region with their disk; choices are revealed simultaneously, and each group moves to its chosen region. Choosing the King’s region or the region being vacated sends that player’s pieces to their court instead. The taboo prevents taking pieces out of the King’s region, and Castillo cannot be emptied with this card.
answers.evidence: Stack 4—Movement gives affected players, simultaneous disk choices and court result for King’s region/vacated region; taboo and Castillo restriction follow.

answers.answer: Royal Adviser moves the King to a neighboring region, at most one region away. The King card may put him in any region except the Castillo.
answers.evidence: Royal Adviser: “neighboring region ... no more than one region away”; King card: “any region except Castillo.”

answers.answer: The Court moves two of your own Caballeros from the provinces to your court. This is separate from the 4-stack card’s normal deployment of up to four from court to the board; either complete activity may be done first.
answers.evidence: The Court: “two of your own Caballeros from provinces to court”; separate from ordinary up-to-four deployment, either activity can go first.

answers.answer: All players choose regions secretly on their disks and reveal simultaneously. A uniquely chosen region is scored under normal rules; if multiple players chose the same region, it is not scored.
answers.evidence: Stack 4: all players choose secretly and reveal simultaneously; score each uniquely chosen region; duplicate choice is not scored.

answers.answer: You may move all your own Caballeros from one origin region, distribute them among other regions and/or Castillo, and return some to the original region. The origin cannot be the King’s region or Castillo; destinations cannot be the King’s region, but may be Castillo.
answers.evidence: Intrigue—“All your own Caballeros from one region”: distribute among other regions and/or Castillo; may return some to original; origins exclude King and Castillo; destinations exclude King.

answers.answer: The normal deployment of up to one plus up to two additional Caballeros from court permits up to three total. The normal one must go to a region adjacent to the King and/or Castillo; the two additional pieces may go to any non-King regions and/or Castillo.
answers.evidence: Intrigue—“Two more from court”: up to two additional; “With the normal one, up to three enter ... only the normal one requires adjacency.”

answers.answer: You may choose only one of the two special alternatives, not both. The normal up-to-one deployment still applies.
answers.evidence: Intrigue choice card: “Choose one of the preceding special actions, not both. Normal deployment still applies.”

answers.answer: Move up to five own and/or foreign Caballeros, but all must come from one origin region. They may be distributed to other non-King regions and/or Castillo.
answers.evidence: Intrigue—“Up to five from one region”: own and/or foreign from one origin, to other non-King regions and/or Castillo.

answers.answer: You may move up to three other players’ Caballeros, may use multiple non-King board-region origins, and may not include your own pieces or take any from Castillo. Destinations may be any non-King regions and/or Castillo.
answers.evidence: Intrigue—“Any three foreign”: up to three other players’ Caballeros, multiple origins, never from Castillo; destinations any non-King regions and/or Castillo.

answers.answer: “Any three” allows up to three own and/or foreign Caballeros from any non-King origin regions (multiple origins allowed) to any non-King regions and/or Castillo. “Any four” allows up to four own and/or foreign from any non-King origin regions into other non-King regions and/or Castillo.
answers.evidence: Intrigue table: any three from any non-King origin regions to any non-King regions/Castillo; any four has same ownership/origin flexibility but destinations are “other” non-King regions/Castillo.

answers.answer: Move up to two of your own plus up to two foreign Caballeros, as separate ownership allowances, from any non-King board regions; multiple origins are allowed. Do not take them from Castillo. They may go to any non-King regions and/or Castillo.
answers.evidence: Intrigue—“Two own and two foreign”: up to two own plus two foreign, multiple origins, never take from Castillo; any non-King destinations and/or Castillo.

answers.answer: Move up to four Caballeros, your own only, from any non-King origin regions into other non-King regions and/or Castillo.
answers.evidence: Intrigue—“Any four of your own”: up to four own only, from any non-King origins into other non-King regions and/or Castillo.

answers.answer: On the 4-stack secret-choice scoring card, a player may choose any of the nine board regions, including the King’s region, but not Castillo. By comparison, the card letting its player pick one location to score allows any region including the King’s region or Castillo.
answers.evidence: Stack 4 says disk permits nine board regions including King’s region but not Castillo. Stack 2 says pick any region including King’s region or Castillo.

answers.answer: The two mobile scoreboards start beside the board. The place-or-move action can introduce a scoreboard from beside the board or move one already on the board to a different region.
answers.evidence: Setup: “Place both mobile scoreboards beside the board.” Stack 4: introduce from beside board or move one already on it.

answers.answer: Each player receives their color’s thirteen power cards, numbered 1 through 13.
answers.evidence: Components: “values 1–13 per color”; Setup: “each player their color’s thirteen power cards.”
